extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and readers studying craft (especially short-story and literary fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply Flannery O'Connor's craft principles for fiction: using sensory detail and 'manners' (concrete behavior) to reveal deeper 'mystery' and moral/anagogical meaning without preaching. Primarily aimed at writers of short stories and literary fiction seeking how to make surface action carry thematic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central Distinction — Mystery and Manners
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two qualities that make fiction. One is the sense of mystery and the other is the sense of manners." The writer's job: approach the deepest mysteries through the surfaces of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery = the deepest meanings; ultimate questions; the unsayable. Manners = observable surface; how people actually behave; concrete reality. The two must work together: manners furnish the concrete material through which mystery is revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction Operates Through the Senses
rubrics_metrics.description: "No reader who doesn't actually experience the story is going to believe anything the fiction writer tells him." Concrete sensory experience is the only path to larger meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the story perceptible through what characters see, hear, smell, taste, and touch. Avoid telling or abstract summary; show through sensory detail. Anti-pattern: relying on exposition or abstract statements to convey significance instead of embodied perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Anagogical Vision (layers of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reality has multiple layers—literal, moral, allegorical, anagogical (spiritual). Quality fiction makes the literal so present that the deeper layers shimmer beneath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the literal (surface events and behavior) with enough concreteness that moral, allegorical, or spiritual readings feel earned rather than imposed. Do not announce levels; allow readers to sense the layers through concrete detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners First (raw materials are in manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The raw materials of a story are found in manners, not mystery. Manners are what we see with our eyeballs when we look out at the world of human interaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from gesture, speech, posture, place, and everyday behavior rather than big themes. Big themes (love, sin, grace) should be emergent results of observed manners, not starting points. Anti-pattern: beginning with a theme and crafting scenes to preach it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional Specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fiction writer is concerned with everything human — that's what manners is — and the more particular he can be, the better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific details of place, class, era, and local custom to ground scenes; particularity breeds universality. Avoid generic or flattened settings; specificity supplies credibility and texture that enable broader meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Grotesque (use of exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Connor defends Southern Gothic/grotesque writing: "to the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost-blind you draw large and startling figures." Fiction's exaggeration serves to make truths visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration, grotesque elements, or startling figures can be legitimate tools when they reveal truth otherwise unseen. Ensure the grotesque 'earns its place' by contributing to perception of deeper reality rather than serving mere shock or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Vision Without Moralism
rubrics_metrics.description: O'Connor's fiction has theological/moral depth but never preaches; theme emerges through embodied action, not didactic statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed moral or spiritual vision in character behavior and consequence rather than announcing judgments. Avoid explicit sermonizing; let moral implications arise from what characters do and undergo.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Reader's Senses (first characteristic of fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first characteristic of fiction is that it deals with reality through what can be seen, heard, smelt, tasted, and touched."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sensory, embodied detail to make the fictional world real to the reader. Evaluate prose by whether readers can 'experience' the scene rather than merely be told about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Are the manners specific?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the manners (place, class, era, gesture, speech) in the work are specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity of manners indicates authenticity and provides the concrete material for meaning to emerge. Vague or generic behavior weakens the story's capacity to reveal deeper truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Does the surface action carry larger weight?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the surface action in the story conveys or supports larger thematic or metaphysical weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface events should resonate beyond themselves and imply or instantiate larger meanings. Anti-pattern: surface incidents that remain isolated and fail to suggest deeper significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Is the moral vision implicit, not announced?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that moral or theological vision is implicit in action rather than explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fiction reveals moral insight through consequence, behavior, and characterization. If the writer explicitly declares morals, the work drifts toward moralism and loses subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Does the work shock the reader into seeing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the writing provokes recognition or a sudden insight in the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective stories can 'shock' by making truths visible in fresh ways. This shock should illuminate rather than gratuitously startle; it should facilitate perception of the mystery via the manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Is the strangeness/grotesque earning its place?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether any strangeness or grotesque elements are justified by their contribution to the story's insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grotesque or exaggerated elements must serve the work's moral or perceptual aims. Avoid using grotesque features merely for sensationalism; they should reveal rather than distract.
